arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: David Goldberg argued the law abridges freedom of speech. He stated it reaches core First Amendment activity. He claimed this activity is unrelated to the government's preventative purpose.

The state argued the law targets virtual places where children congregate. It cited the 2008 decision to prohibit access to commercial social networking sites. It framed this as a logical extension of physical location bans.

Justices probed the line between permissible and impermissible restrictions. They asked about monitoring technology and specific contact scenarios. They tested the law against historical First Amendment principles.

paragraphs: North Carolina law prohibits registered sex offenders from accessing commercial social networking websites. the side that brought the case claims this restriction infringes on First Amendment rights. The state argues the ban prevents contact with minors online.

sections.heading: What each side wants

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the law reaches vast swaths of protected speech. He claims it is not narrowly tailored to the government's purpose.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if a state could impose this restriction as a parole condition.

Justice Alito asked if banning a kidnapper from visiting a nursery school violates the First Amendment. He used this to test the scope of the restriction. He also asked if monitoring apps that disclose communication with minors are permissible. Justice Ginsburg asked if contacting a known minor online is a crime.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between public safety and free speech online. It determines whether states can ban specific categories of citizens from using the internet. The outcome shapes how governments regulate digital access for convicted individuals. It impacts the right to access information and communicate in public forums.
